extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, judges, and other patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes Federal Circuit decisions articulating legal standards for patent validity, claim construction, inequitable conduct, jurisdiction, and related doctrines (obviousness, written description, indefiniteness, etc.). Useful for practitioners applying these standards in litigation and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success (obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding of obviousness does not require a guarantee of success—only a reasonable expectation of success is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certainty and absolute predictability are not required. Prior art that demonstrates successes (not only failures) across relevant embodiments can support a reasonable expectation of success. Courts should assess whether a skilled artisan would have had a reasonable expectation of achieving the claimed result (e.g., a 2-log increase across serotypes, or achieving a claimed dosage/form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper motivation to combine prior art references requires more than simply recognizing that two alternative arrangements or elements were known in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclosure must provide reasons why a skilled artisan would substitute or combine one element for another or what advantages would result. Mere existence of possible arrangements in prior art is insufficient. Expert testimony must articulate why a POSA would be motivated to combine references; conclusory testimony is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious-to-try analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: An obviousness combination cannot be justified solely because an element was 'obvious to try' if there is no reasoned expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although references disclosing alternative approaches may make something 'obvious to try,' the PTAB/Federal Circuit requires more—reasons to select one approach and a reasonable expectation that the approach would work. The fact that a reference discloses multiple options (e.g., Briggs discloses 3D coordinates and angular directions) does not alone supply motivation to combine with another reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSA) in obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior art must be considered from the viewpoint of a POSA, including background knowledge and tendency to modify or combine references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should avoid a siloed, rigid, or one-by-one analysis of references. The analysis should allow consideration of a POSA's background knowledge and how a POSA would understand motivations to modify or combine prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of prior art protocols lacking safety/efficacy data
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of safety and efficacy data in prior art protocols does not justify discarding those protocols when evaluating obviousness, especially if the claims do not require safety or efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior art protocol need not itself be shown flawed for a POSA to alter it. The lack of trial data alone does not preclude using protocols to inform obviousness if a POSA would have reason to modify or combine the protocols with other references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art disclosure pointing to an optimal range or preference does not necessarily 'teach away' from other ranges or alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'optimal range' cited in prior art is not, by itself, a criticism of all other sizes/values and therefore may not constitute teaching away. Courts must assess whether the prior art criticizes, discredits, or discourages the claimed approach, not merely prefers a particular parameter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (objective indicia) analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary considerations — unexpected results, industry praise, long-felt need (and the effect of blocking patents), and commercial success — must be properly analyzed in the obviousness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts should evaluate and weigh secondary considerations appropriately; failure or misanalysis can require remand. Guidance includes examining unexpected results relative to claim scope, how blocking patents affect long-felt need, and whether commercial success is causally tied to the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness: reasonable certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are definite if they inform, with reasonable certainty, those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent contradictions across limitations do not automatically render a claim indefinite if it is possible to meet both limitations. Measurement technique disputes (e.g., particle-size techniques) require more than an outlier discrepancy to show indefiniteness; an isolated outlier measurement is not evidence that different techniques would typically yield materially different results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (possession)
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description is met when the disclosure reasonably conveys to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter as of the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specification need not expressly recite a claimed subrange if the disclosure (including explicit disclosure of endpoints) reasonably conveys possession. The amount of detail required depends on the predictability of the art (less detail required for more predictable/electromechanical arts). Compare to prior precedent (Wertheim, Blaser, Kolmes) when analyzing subrange support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of claimed ranges and subranges
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed narrower subrange can be supported by broader disclosed ranges when the disclosure reasonably conveys possession of the subrange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should assess whether the specification's disclosed ranges and endpoints reasonably convey the narrower claimed range; predictability of the technology and whether both endpoints are disclosed are relevant factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequitable conduct: materiality and intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Inequitable conduct requires evaluation of both materiality (but-for or per se material in case of affirmative egregious misconduct) and specific intent to deceive, which are distinct requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must separately find materiality and intent. For affirmative egregious misconduct, misrepresentations may be per se material; otherwise, courts must determine but-for materiality. Intent should be evaluated in the aggregate — a pattern of lack of candor may demonstrate intent. Courts should not treat purposeful misrepresentations as mere gross negligence without considering specific intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unclean hands doctrine in patent litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Unclean hands can bar a party from obtaining relief when the party engaged in deceitful or reprehensible conduct that has an immediate and necessary connection to the claims for relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of conduct supporting unclean hands include failure to disclose related patent applications, obstructing discovery, evasive testimony, and false testimony contradicted by contemporaneous evidence. The misconduct must be directly relevant to the litigation and affect the opposing party's ability to litigate the issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral order doctrine test (appellate jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: To fall within the collateral order doctrine, an order must (1) conclusively determine the disputed question, (2) resolve an important issue completely separate from the merits, and (3) be effectively unreviewable on appeal from a final judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A district court's preliminary denial of a motion (e.g., denying dismissal due to inadequate record) that does not make a conclusive determination does not satisfy the doctrine; appellate jurisdiction is therefore lacking in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal jurisdiction (specific jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific personal jurisdiction requires that the defendant purposefully directed activities at the forum and that the action arises out of or relates to the defendant's forum activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insufficient contacts with the forum (e.g., mere online listings or generalized contacts) can preclude specific jurisdiction; courts examine purposeful direction and the causal nexus between the forum contacts and the asserted claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting and functional limitations (mutually exclusive concern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in the same patent may recite different ordered combinations of limitations and need not be totally consistent; functional limitations (e.g., 'substantially rigid portion') need not have identical boundaries across independent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeling claims as 'mutually exclusive' is not a basis for indefiniteness if each claim, construed in context, informs a POSA of its scope with reasonable certainty. Functional claim terms are construed by their function and need not specify exact boundaries so long as the construction is consistent across claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation in polymorph/form claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a skilled artisan would have a reasonable expectation of obtaining a claimed polymorphic form depends on whether prior art provides processes, characterizations, or routine assays that would lead to detection or production of that form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior art discloses a process producing a crystalline form and characterization would routinely reveal the claimed polymorph (with expert support), a reasonable expectation may be found. Contrast with cases where prior art consistently produced a different form and lacked guidance on conditions to obtain the claimed form (e.g., Grunenthal).
